title: Double Correction Framework for Denoising Recommendation

problem.claim: Implicit feedback is commonly used in recommender systems, but real-world implicit feedback contains noisy samples that impair precise user preference learning.

gap.claim: Dropping high-loss samples can mistake optimization-instability or hard samples for noise and can worsen data sparsity by discarding potentially useful data.

narrative_sequence.summary: Implicit feedback is widely used in recommender systems because of its availability and generality.
Implicit feedback contains noisy samples that affect precise user preference learning.
A common approach drops samples with high training losses during model training.
High losses may reflect optimization instability or difficult samples, and dropping noisy samples can aggravate data sparsity.

source_observation.claim: High training loss is not uniquely attributable to noisy feedback.

interpretation.claim: Loss-based sample filtering can remove difficult but informative examples when optimization effects and noise are not separated.

application.claim: Denoising methods should distinguish noise from optimization instability and hard samples before discarding data.

exception.claim: The supplied units do not specify when loss-based filtering is reliable.

source_observation.claim: Dropping noisy samples reduces the amount of training data and can aggravate data sparsity.

interpretation.claim: Denoising should account for the value of retaining and exploiting available data.

application.claim: Prefer denoising strategies that mitigate harmful feedback while preserving useful observations where possible.

exception.claim: The supplied units do not describe how to preserve data while removing noise.

unknowns: The proposed double correction framework is not described.
No experiments, datasets, baselines, metrics, or quantitative results are supplied.
No theoretical analysis or implementation details are supplied.
